ORAL ANSWERS TO QUESTIONS 
Enquiry reports on Helicopter Crashes 
*541.    SHRI AMAR SINGH:† 
SHRIMATI SUKHBUNS KAUR: 
Will the Minister of CIVIL AVIATION be pleased to state: 
(a) the number of choppers (civilian) which crashed during the last three years 
alongwith the causes of each crash; 
(b) what action Government have taken in the light of findings of enquiries 
conducted in this regard; 
(c) whether Government's attention has been drawn to the recent statement 
by lAF's Director-General (Inspection and Safety) after the recent mishap resulting 
in the deaths of two Ministers of Haryana Government to the effect that stringent 
norms for selection of pilots and helicopters and a review of Civil Aviation Rules 
enacted in 1934 can go a long way in preventing the mishaps; and 
(d) if so, what is Government's reaction in regard thereto and by when, the 
rules are likely to be reviewed? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE OF THE MINISTRY OF CIVIL AVIATION 
(SHRI PRAFUL PATEL): (a) to (d) A Statement is laid on the Table of the 
House. 
Statement 
(a) During the last 3 years i.e. 2002 to 2005 till date there had been 18 
accidents to Indian Civil Registered Helicopters (Choppers). The causes of these 
accidents are given in Statement-I (See below). 
(b) Safety recommendations emanating from investigation of various 
aircraft accidents and incidents are followed up by Directorate General of Civil 
Aviation (DGCA) for implementation with the concerned agencies so as to 
prevent recurrence of similar accident s/incidents. A Standing Committee 
headed by Director General of Civil Aviation periodically monitors the progress of 
implementation of the recommendations made by various Courts/Committees of 
Inquiries. Besides, Flight Inspector of Pilots of DGCA carries out periodic 
proficiency and standardization checks of pilots and Safety Audit team of 
DGCA carry out periodical safety audit of operation and maintenance 
organization. A Helicopter Group has been constituted by DGCA on 17.09.2003 
to look after the maintenance and operations of Helicopters until creation of 
separate Helicopter Cell in DGCA. 
(c) and (d) Yes, Sir. However, DGCA has not received any official

Space crunch at major airports 
*542. SHRI TARIQ ANWAR: Will the Minister of CIVIL AVIATION be pleased 
to state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that the Indira Gandhi International Airport and other major 
airports are facing space crunch; 
(b) if so, the reasons therefor; and 
(c) the steps taken in this regard? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE OF THE MINISTRY OF CIVIL AVIATION (SHRI 
PRAFUL PATEL): (a) to (c) A Statement is laid on the Table of the House. 
Statement 
(a) to (c) Of late, Civil Aviation Sector in India has registered rapid traffic growth in 
aircraft movements, passengers and cargo. At some airports including Indira Gandhi 
International Airport, New Delhi the infrastructure development both at air side and 
terminals has not kept pace with the 
15 

RAJYA SABHA [3 May, 2005] 
traffic growth. Such airports are experiencing space crunch in terms of capacity 
both on airside and terminals. As a result, airlines and passengers are experiencing 
difficulty particularly during peak hours. Government with a view to add capacity to 
meet the growing demands, has taken the following steps:- (i) Restructuring and 
modernization of Delhi and Mumbai airports through public private partnership 
to develop them as world class airports, (ii) A decision has also been taken to 
develop tentatively selected 25 non-metro airports focusing on airside and city side 
development to world class standards, (iii) To strengthen the airport 
infrastructure, private sector is being encouraged to promote Greenfield airports and 
complement the efforts of Airports Authority of India (AAI) in the development of 
airport infrastructure in the country. Government has already approved setting up of 
Greenfield airports at Shamshabad near Hyderabad, Devanahalli near Bangalore 
and Mopa in Goa. (iv) Extension and modification of Terminal-IB at Mumbai 
airport and modification of Terminal-IB at Delhi Airport have been taken up by 
AAI. Extension and renovation of Terminal-2B at Mumbai airport has also 
been approved by AAI. (v) Steps such as introduction of Common User 
Terminal Equipment (CUTE) for smooth check-in, introduction of Air Traffic 
Flow Management (ATFM), provision of high speed taxi-ways, parallel taxi-ways, 
additional parking bays are also planned at Delhi and Mumbai to expand airside 
capacity and terminal facilities.

*543. SHRIMATI SUKHBUNS KAUR: Will the Minister of FINANCE be pleased 
to state: 
(a) whether any rules or guidelines have been laid down for management 
20 

[3 May, 2005] RAJYA SABHA 
and appropriation of the National investment Fund; 
(b) if so, the details thereof; 
(c) what is the present corpus of this fund and the expected annual returns 
therefrom and how far these returns are higher than the dividend market price 
ratio of the PSUs in raising this fund; and 
(d) what steps are being taken to ensure that the returns therefrom do not turn 
negative as it happened lately in the case of the Unit Trust of India? 
THE MINISTER OF FINANCE (SHRI P. CHIDAMBARAM): (a) to (d) A 
Statement is laid on the Table of the House. 
Statement 
(a) and (b) Government has decided that with effect from 1 st Aprii 2005 the 
realisation from disinvestment of Public Sector Enterprises (PSEs), which are 
credited to the Consolidated Fund of India will be appropriated from the 
Consolidated Fund of India for the creation of the National Investment Fund 
(NIF). The NIF would be professionally managed by selected Public Sector 
Financial entities, with the requisite experience, to provide sustainable returns to 
the Government without affecting the corpus. The income from the NIF would be 
credited to the Consolidated Fund of India and would thereafter be appropriated to 
finance selected social sector schemes, which promote education and health care. 
A part of the Fund w ill be used for capital investment in selected profitable and 
revivable PSEs that yield adequate returns, in order to enlarge their capital base 
and to finance their expansion/diversification. 
(c) The corpus of the NIF would depend upon the level of disinvestment during 
the current financial year and thereafter. The annual returns from the NIF will be 
market determined. However, since the NIF will be actively managed by selected 
professional Public Sector Financial Entities, with the requisite expertise, the 
returns are expected to be good. 
(d) The Net Asset Value of a market-based fund varies in the short term with the 
fluctuations in the market. However, any adverse fluctuation in the short term gets 
averaged out over the long term through growth of the economy and 
development and deepening of the financial markets. Appropriate agreements 
would be put in place with the Public Sector Financial Ent ities, managing the 
NIF, to facilitate the long term growth of the corpus.

(a) whether taking note of their incorrect investment pattern in oil and gas sector, 
Central Public Sector Undertakings viz. ONGC, IOCL, HPCL, BPCL, GAIL and OIL 
have been urged to improve their intrinsic competitiveness and professional 
functioning. 
(b) if so, whether during discussions in mid-term appraisal it was felt that there is a 
need to restructure the oil companies to attain sectoral objectives;

(d) the steps being taken to implement them? 
THE MINISTER OF PETROLEUM AND NATURAL GAS (SHRIMANI 
SHANKAR AIYAR): (a) to (d) A Statement is laid on the Table of the House. 
Statement 
(a) to (d) The Mid Term Appraisal Document of the Planning Commission for the Tenth 
Plan (2002—07) is yet to be finalized. However, their draft document for the Mid 
Term Appraisal has made the following recommendations:- 
I. Restructure the oil and gas CPSUs in order to promote effective 
competition. 
II. Review the current pricing of crude oil (both domestic and imported), 
natural gas and all its components, petroleum products and pipeline 
transportation and other services. 
III. Introduce price competition in all petroleum products. Impose 
universal service obligations by requiring a percentage of sales in 
notified areas but allow differential pricing in different markets to 
reflect cost of supply. States ma y choose to subsidize prices in 
remote areas. 
IV. Bid out subsidies for LPG and Kerosene. 
V. Encourage competing private par ticipation in each element of the 
oil and gas industry (exploration and production, refining, 
marketing). 
VI. Rationalise the tax and duty structure prevailing in the oil and gas sector. 
VII. Declare authorized enduses (as long as demand exceeds supply) for domestic 
natural gas and piped natural gas imports. Allow the market to determine the 
price of natural gas for these recognized enduses. LNG may be sold for any 
enduse and could complete with natural gas to meet any residual demand for 
the authorized enduses. 
VIII. Increase emphasis on acquiring equity oil and gas abroad. Develop capacity and 
structures that provide better assessment/control of commercial and political 
risks of such investments. 
IX   Increase emphasis on transnational pipelines and LNG imports. 
31 

RAJYA SABHA [3 May, 2005] 
X Develop transportation and distribution assets in the oil and gas sector that 
provide services under common carrier principles applicable to natural 
monopolies. 
XI. Modify the Petroleum and Natural Gas Regulatory Bill, 2004 to include 
regulation of upstream sector. 
XII. Allow foreign operators to bring technology and investment to recover oil/gas 
from currently abandoned and/or marginal fields on economic 
considerations. 
The recommendations are being examined by the Ministry for sending replies to the 
Planning Commission for further necessary action.

*546.    SHRI RAMA MUNI REDDY SIRIGIREDDY: 
SHRI K. RAMA MOHANA RAO: 
Will the Minister of PETROLEUM AND NATURAL GAS be pleased to 
state: 
(a) whether India have any long-term contract with the oil producing 
countries i.e. OPEC; 
(b) if so, the details of the countries and contracts that India entered into 
with these countries; 
(c) if not, whether India had made any efforts at the recently held Asian Round 
Table Conference on Oil Cooperation; 
(d) whether any countries have agreed to India's proposal of long-term oil 
deals;

country? 
THE MINISTER OF PETROLEUM AND NATURAL GAS (SHRI MANI 
SHANKAR AIYAR): (a) to (e) Indian public and private oil companies buy 
crude oil on term contracts from National Oil Companies of countries like Saudi 
Arabia, Iran, Kuwait and Abu Dhabi, who are members of OPEC. Term 
contracts are generally for one year and, in most cases, the contract is renewable 
automatically. Public sector oil companies factor in longer-term contracts in 
their purchase arrangements, as appropriate, but it may be noted that long-term 
contracts only provide for assurance of supplies; prices are linked to periodic 
variations in international markets. 
The question of longer-term supply contracts was raised at the first Round 
Table of Asian Oil Ministers on regional cooperation in the oil and gas economy 
held in New Delhi on 6 January, 2005 which was attended by 
Ministers/representatives from Iran, Japan, Malaysia, Oman, Qatar, Saudi 
Arabia, JAE, Kuwait, China, Korea besides host India. As there are both 
advantages and disadvantages to longe r term supply contracts, the question 
remains under consideration both bilaterally and in forums such as the Round 
Table.

4198. SHRI RAM NATH KOVIND: Will the Minister of FINANCE be

THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF FINANCE (SHRI 
S.S. PALANIMANICKAM): (a) VAT has been introduced in 21 States/Union 
Territories w.e.f. 1st April, 2005. 
(b) VAT is a simple, transparent, multi-stage tax with input tax credit, which 
eliminates cascading of taxes and avoids consequent price escalation. Further, 
as decided by the Empowered committ ee of State Finance Ministers, it is 
expected that a number of State level taxes on 
62 

[3 May, 2005] RAJYA SABHA 
purchase or sales of goods like State sales tax, turnover tax, purchase tax, 
additional sales tax, surcharge, entry tax (not in lieu of Octroi) will be subsumed 
in VAT. Hence, VAT will decrease mu ltiplicity of taxes and ultimately be 
beneficial to common public. 
(c) Information is being collected and will be laid on the Table of the 
House. 
(d) Under Entry 54 of List II (State List) in the Seventh Schedule to the 
Constitution of India, tax on sale or pruchase of goods is a State subject. A 
process of debate and discussion for the reform of domestic trade taxes was 
initiated in 1994 by the State/Union Territory finance Ministers. Serious discussions 
to introduce a Value Added Tax (VAT), replacing the existing Sales Tax systems 
of the States, were initiated at a mee ting of the State/ Union Territory Chief 
Ministers called by Dr. Manmohan Singh, the then Union Finance Minister, in 
December, 1995. In a subsequent meeting of Chief Ministers held on the 16th 
November, 1999, it was decided that a State level VAT should be intr oduced. 
This was reiterated in subsequent conferences of the Chief Minsiters held on 
the 22nd June, 2000 and 5th July, 2001. An empowered Committee of State 
Finance Ministers was also constituted on the recommendation of Chief 
Ministers in July, 2000, inter-alia, to monitor the process of introduction of 
VAT. In the meeting of the Empowered Committee of State Finance Ministers 
held on the 18th June', 2004, there was broad consensus to implement State 
level VAT w.e.f. the 1st April, 2005.

Higher customs duty on fixed phone instruments 
4216.   SHRIMATI PREMA CARIAPPA:  
SHRIMATI KAMLA MANHAR: 
Will the Minister of FINANCE be pleased to state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that fixed phone instruments attract a higher customs and 
excise duty as compared to mobile phones;

RAJYA SABHA [3 May, 2005]

THE MINISTER OF STATE IN TH E MINISTRY OF FINANCE (SHRI 
S.S. PALANIMANICKAM) : (a) and (b ) The customs and excise duty 
structure for fixed phone instruments and mobile phones is as follows:— 
(i) Both fixed line telephones and mobile phones attract nil basic 
costoms duty and 4% additional duty of customs, w.e.f. 1.3.2005. 
(ii) Cellular phones and radio trunking terminals are fully exempt from 
excise duty. Other telephone sets including fixed line telephones attract 
excise duty at the Cenvat rate of 16%. 
Exemption from excise duty was given to cellular phones mainly to reduce 
the cost so as to reduce the incentive for smuggling.

telephones and mobile phones.Only 4% additional duty of customs under 
section 3 (5) of the Customs Tariff Act is levied on both fixed line telephones 
and mobile phones. Fixed phones attract excise duty at 16%.Telephone 
manufacturers can take credit of excise duty/additional duty of customs (CVD) 
paid on parts/components for manufacture of telephone sets. The excise duty 
paid on telephone sets is also eligible to be taken as credit under the Cenvat 
Credit Rules, 2004, by service providers, for payment of service tax on 
output services.

Removal of Sales tax consequent to introduction of VAT 
†4228. SHRI RAVI SHANKAR PRASAD:  
SHRI RAM JETHMALANI: 
Will the Minister of FINANCE be pleased to state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that the purpose behind introducing new tax-system in the 
form of VAT in the country is to increase the amount of tax in the average of Gross 
Domestic Product; 
(b) if not, Government's reaction in this regard; 
(c) whether it is a fact that VAT is a substitute of the sales-tax in the States; 
(d) whether it is a fact that certain conditions to remove 4 per cent sales tax levied by 
the Centre are still in force; and 
(e) if so, the details of the conditions and the reasons for not removing Central Sales 
Tax simultaneously while levying VAT? 
† Original notice of the question was received in Hindi.  
86 

[3 May, 2005] RAJYA SABHA 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF FINANCE (SHRI 
S.S. PALANIMANICKAM). (a) and (b) VAT is a tax intended to replace the 
State Sales Tax. Hence, it is a State subject. The revenue generated from it will 
be collected and retained by the State Governments. The Central Government is 
only playing the role of facilitator in this tax reform process. 
(c) Yes, Sir. 
(d) and (e) At present, Central Sales Tax @ 4 per cent is levied on inter-State 
sale of goods. A Tax Information Exchange System to track the movement of 
goods is being put in place, which is a pre-requisite for phasing out the Central Sales 
Tax. As it is expected that the Tax Information Exchange System shall be operational 
only after some time, it was decided in the meeting of the Empowered 
Committee of State Finance Ministers held on 2nd November, 2004 that the Central 
Sales Tax would continue, as at present, during 2005-06 and that the Empowered 
Committee would review the position next year and advise the Central Government 
on this matter.

Statement 
Joint Statement of conclusions arrived at after the visit of the Union 
Minister for Panchayati Raj and Petroleum and Natural Gas to 
Karnataka on the 29th April and 1st May, 2005 
Karnataka has championed the noble cause of empowering Panchayats and devolving 
powers to them since decades. 'The State has been at the forefront of the empowerment of all 
three levels of Panchayats so that they function as institutions of local self-Government in 
the letter and spirit of Part IX of the Constitution. The recent measures of the 
Karnataka Government stand testimony to its sustained support to Panchayati Raj 
reform. The amendments made to the karnataka Panchayati Raj Act in October, 2003 and 
the subsequent steps taken to strengthen the Grama Sabha; create and empower Ward 
Sabhas; complete Activity Mapping; and rationalize and simplify schemes entrusted to 
the Panchayats are examples to be emulated countrywide'. The monitoring of the 
actualization of devolution by the Legislative Committees is a significant step in the 
strengthening of Panchayats in the State. The entrustment of schemes by the State 
Government to Panchayats in the current year's budget is a giant step forward in 
matching-the functional transfer with funds. Through 
119 

RAJYA SABHA [3 May, 2005] 
this process, the Panchayats now handle in excess of Rs. 3500 Crores of Plan funds per 
year. However there is a need to both substantially increase the quantum of funds available 
at each level of Panchayats and to untie the bulk of these funds. 
A fresh national impetus has been given to the devolution of powers and responsibilities 
through the Seven Round Tables of State Ministers of Panchayati Raj which arrived 
by consensus, at 150 recommendations pertaining to 18 dimensions of Panchayati 
Raj. Karnataka has initiated implementation of 77 of the 106 recommendations of the 
Round Tables that pertain to it. The Government of Karnataka will address itself with all 
deliberate speed to the remaining recommendations. 
• The challenges before Karnataka is sustaining the pace of reform will require 
effective support and close coordination with the Central Government. In this 
endeavour the State Government of Karnataka and the Union Ministry of 
Panchayati Raj have agreed to accord priority to the following points. 
• Karnataka has devolved through legislation all the 29 matters in the Eleventh 
Schedule of the Constitution to the Panchayats. This functional transfer has 
been further clarified through an Activity Mapping framework, issued in 
August, 2003. This has been followed by the entrustment of all schemes 
pertaining to the activities devolved upon Panchayats to the respective levels, 
in the State Budget of 2005-06. In the letter and spirit of Article 243 G of the 
Constitution, the Government of Karnataka commit itself to following up the 
devolution of functions and funds with the matching devolution of 
functionaries. 
• For Panchayats to effective plan and implement the functions that have been 
devolved upon them it is necessary that funds pertaining to these scheme are 
transferred to them without delay or diversion. Karnataka has already shown 
the way by putting in place a Bank transfer mechanism for transferring funds to 
Gram Panchayats. In continuation of this reform process, it agrees to put in 
place systems that the capable of tracking transfers of funds to 
Panchayats. 
• The Government of Karnataka will consider the establishment of a cadre of 
administrative and technical staff exclusively for PRIs. 
• Karnataka has recently conducted elec tions to the Gram Panchayats 
and is due to conduct elections to the Taluk and Zilla 
120 

[3 May, 2005] RAJYA SABHA 
Panchayats shortly. A new set of elected representatives have assumed office. 
The Ministry of Panchayati Raj shall assist the Government of Karnataka in 
capacity building and training of these representatives. 
• In order to build capacity and leadership among categories for whom seats are 
reserved, Karnataka shall consider favourably the slowing down of the 
reservation cycle so that the option to reserve seats for more than one-term is 
open but it is for the State Legislature to decide the number of terms for which 
seats will remain reserved. 
• The Union Ministry of Panchayati Raj will pursue the devolution of Central funds 
through united block grants, and systemic reform of Centrally sponsored 
Schemes, including the establishment of a Panchayat Empowerment 
Incentive Fund to bring these in conformity with the constitutional provisions 
for good governance at the district and sub-district levels as set out in Part IX read 
with the relevant articles of Part IXA.

SPECIAL MENTIONS 
Need for upgrading B.S.N.L. cellular services in Bangalore 
SHRI B.K. HARIPRASAD (Karnataka): Sir, cellular phones have become the most affordable 
and handy tool for inter-personal communication both in urban and rural areas, rendering 
the conventional landline phones obsolete. 
Bangalore, despite being the cyber capital of India with MNCs and BPO combines 
operating for global clients, is not served well by BSNL in terms of better cellular 
connectivity. The audibility is low and blurred in fringe areas located far away from 
booster-relay towers. In line with the private operators, BSNL should upgrade its cellular 
capabilities in Bangalore 
183 

RAJYA SABHA [3 May, 2005] 
by installing more booster-relay towers. From a modest 1.74 lakh cellular connections in 
2001-02, BSNL has recorded a quantum leap to 52.54 lakh in 2003-04 but has failed to keep 
up with the technological advancements in the area of cellular telephony. The Comptroller 
and Auditor General of India, in his technical performance appraisal report for the year 
2003-04 has observed that BSNL while ushering in new technologies for its cellular network, 
has not discarded the obsolete systems/equipments even now under operation. 
Bangalore, known as the cradle of telecom, IT and BPO ventures is endowed with 
other attributes-biotechnology, tourism-hospitality, floriculture, multi-cuisine food beverage 
outlets-that make it a metropolis of global standards. Considering the enormous telecom 
revenue potential that Bangalore holds forth, BSNL should act fast and deliver. 
SHRI JANARDHANA POOJARY (Karnataka): Sir, I associate with the hon. Member. 
Concern over distress sale of cotton by farmers 
SHRIMATI SUKHBUNS KAUR (Punjab): During the last cotton crop season (kharif 
2004), the Union Government fixed minimum support price for cotton. Due to good cotton 
crop, cotton prices crashed in the market, when the Cotton Corporation of India failed to lift the 
cotton stocks resulting in grave suffering to farmers. Serious efforts of Punjab and other 
State Governments and fixation of MSP resulted in substantial increase in area under cotton 
cultivation over the last two years but the remunerative MSP for cotton failed to give the desired 
relief and advantage to the farmers and non-lifting of cotton by CCI is leading the farmers 
to resort to distress sales and even suicides. The Government should, therefore, direct 
the Cotton Corporation of India to intervene proactively and lift surplus cotton from the market 
to relieve the farmers of the grave burden. 
SHRI DATTA MEGHE (Maharashtra): Sir, I associate myself with the hon. Member. 
Demand for early clearance of Rowghat mines, Chhattisgarh 
SHRI MOTILAL VORA(Chhattisgarh): Sir, the future of Bhilai Steel Plant to a great extent 
depends on the clearance of Rowghat mines. The BSP management has been vigorously 
pursuing the issue of clearance of Rowghat mines with the Government but not much 
headway has been made. The State Government has forwarded BSP's application for forestry 
184 

[3 May, 2005]             RAJYA SABHA 
clearance to the Ministry of Environment  and Forests on the basis of revised 
Regional Mines Development Plan and Feasibility Report for Rowghat 
submitted by the Indian Bureau of Mines, Nagpur. 
In the revised Regional Mines Development Plan for Rowghat to the State 
Government, the IBM has recommended an area of 2,409 hectare land for 
exploitation for mining and setting up of a 14 MT crushing, screening and 
beneficiation plant at Rowghat. BSP sources need 300 rakes of iron ore from its 
mines each month. Unless Bhilai gets statutory clearance for Rowghat at the 
earliest, BSP will have to purchase iron ore from 2,011 onwards, the landed cost 
of which will be prohibitive and will neutralise a major portion of profits. SAIL and 
Bhilai are waiting with bated breath for Mission Rowghat to bear fruit-at best an 
early forestry clearance. 
Need to give prominence to Dr. Ambedkar foundation 
SHRIMATI SYEDA ANWARA TAIMUR (Assa m): Sir, in recognition of the 
distinguished services rendered by Dr. Ambedkar, the Government of India 
commemorated centenary year of his birth in 1991 as the Year of Social 
Justice. In his fond memory, the Government of India set up a Foundation in 
the year 1992 in the name of Dr . B.R. Ambedkar as an autonomous 
organisation, under the aegis of the Ministry of Social Justice and Empowerment 
with a corpus fund of Rs. 74 crores. Now, the fund available with the 
Foundation is Rs. 170 crores. 
In spite of the Foundation having sufficient fund, the activities of the 
Foundation are not expanded and the budget earmarked for the year 2004-05, 
that is, Rs. 3.91 crores could not be spent fully, not even half of the grants were 
spent, out of the grants allocated for the last financial year, and only Rs. 1.2 
crores could be spent. 
In recognition of his services, there are two awards supposed to be given 
every year, i.e., (i) Dr. Ambedkar National Award for the uplift of the weaker 
sections and (ii) Dr. Ambedkar International Award for Social Change. But Dr. 
Ambedkar National Award for the uplift of the weaker sections has not been 
given by the Dr. Ambedkar Foundation since the year 1999, and Dr. Ambedkar 
International Award for Social Change has not been given by the Foundation 
since the year 2001, in spite of having  sufficient funds with the Foundation. A 
scheme of Dr. Ambedkar Samajik Samata Kendra Yojana for construction of Dr. 
Ambedkar bhawans all over India, which was started in the year 2003-2004, has not 
been implemented. 
This attitude towards the Foundation will send wrong signals among the 
followers of ideology and philosophy of Dr. B.R. Ambedkar. 
185 

RAJYA SABHA [3 May, 2005] 
I, therefore, urge upon the Government to pay more attention towards the Dr. 
Ambedkar Foundation so as not to allow any criticism in the matter. Thank you.

Demand for rectification in the census of 2001 in respect of scheduled 
caste population in the country 
SHRI R.S. GAVAI (Maharashtra): Sir, New Buddhists are a religious group 
which had come into existence in 1956 as a result of the view of conversion of 
Scheduled Castes under the leadership of Dr. Babasaheb Ambedkar. 
The Constitution (Scheduled Castes) Order, 1950 as amended by 
Amendment No. 15 of 1990, mentions that change in religion has not altered their 
social and economic conditions and whatever concessions are available to 
Scheduled Castes have been extended to New Buddhists. 
This was to be strictly followed in the census survey report. But contrary to this, 
the census report of 2001 disclosed the population of Scheduled Caste at very 
lower side in comparison to the census report of 1991. 
Due to wrong recording of New Buddhists in the list of Scheduled Castes, the 
population of Scheduled Castes is reduced. This is reflected in the election of 
Gram Panchayats in Maharashtra. The same  effect will be there in local self-
authorities, Assemblies and Parliament  elections. Therefore, the same may 
be rectified. 
I, therefore, draw the attention of the hon. Prime Minister and the hon. Home 
Minister for appropriate action in this respect.

Chairman, Sir, the environment protection should be the prime aim of this Bill, but 
when we view the Bill there is nothing regarding protection of the environment. 
Regarding certain restrictions which are given in this Bill, there is only one thing 
that is shown in Clause 13(8)(a). 
No coastal aquaculture shall be carried on within two hundred metres from the 
High Tide Lines" and (b)" No coastal aquaculture shall be carried

1.00 P.M. 
on in the creeks, rivers and backwaters within the Coastal Regulation Zone declared for 
the time being under the Environment (Protection) Act, 1986". Except this, nothing more is 
given regarding restrictions in this particular Bill. Therefore, the simple thing happening is 
creation of a new authority and giving employment to some people. That is the only thing 
that is happening. It can very well be done by amending the Environment Protection Act, 
1986, itself and including a clause that permission has to be given under certain 
circumstances for this particular coastal aquaculture. Except that, Sir, no protection is given for 
the agriculturists. The problem throughout the coastal area is that some companies like M/s.

who knew that banks were giving money, started this business, but they failed in the 
business. They could not compete with the market price. Therefore, everyone has gone 
except the companies, which have got some money, or which can, by some book-keeping 
methods, show some loss and other things. They are spoiling the entire coastal area. 
Wherever this particular work was started, in that area, drinking water has become saline. 
Villagers in that area are suffering. In the same way, those areas, where these types of farms 
were developed, have become non-agricultural land and agriculturists are going away 
from the villages. No compensation provision has been provided for. Suppose, these 
particular people are allowed to have the same venture after some time, say after five years or 
so, if they go away from that venture, what will happen? Those lands will become non-
agricultural land. Nobody is going to use them. We may be earning crores of rupees, but what 
is the loss that we are causing to our motherland. Entire coastal area is going to become 
fallow land, sandy land and the level of underground drinking water is also going down. In my 
own constituency, that is, Sivaganga Parliamentary constituency, from where I stood for my 
last term, that area Ramnad district, throught out that coastal area, these aquaculture farms 
were created. The entire area, which was having very good water for the drinking purpose, now 
has become saline. They are conducting a study there itself. The State Government is also 
not at all caring about those people. The drinking water is now sold for five rupees for 
ordinary villagers because of these matters. Therefore, the agriculturists are now going away 
from these coastal areas. We can very easily find out these facts from my area itself, from 
Ramnad district, and the coastal area of S.P. Pattinam to the Tondi coastal area and other 
places, like Nambudalai. Therefore, I would like to suggest that the

RAJYA SABHA [3 May, 2005] 
Government should take care of the agriculturists first. Then, they have to take care whether 
the drinking water is going to be spoiled or not. When the hard water, the saline water 
comes inside, automatically, it goes and fills up inland also. It goes even to the level of 60 
kilometres inside the land. I can very well say that even it has come to the level of 90

farmers of aquaculture because we have certain concerns. Sir, in the last ten years,

neglect of agriculture, because of non-investment in the agriculture sector, many 
farmers were given to take up cash crop cultivation. As a part of this tendency, 
they started aquaculture near the creek waters - the water where the seawaters 
meet the fresh water - on the banks of the Krishna and near the Buckingham Canal. 
Lakhs and Lakhs of acres have been brought into aquaculture in that region. In 
the initial stages, because of the freshness of the soil,

with me, in a number of private discussions, that there is a need to change the 
criteria, how to fix up the mechanism to deal with this problem and fix up the criteria 
for identifying the people living below the poverty line. ...(Time-bell).., I will sum 
up, Madam. 
THE VICE-CHAIRMAN (SHRIMATI SARLA MAHSHWARI): Still, you have 
to sum up! 
SHRI R.S. GAVAI: Madam, I will finish within one minute. 
THE VICE-CHAIRMAN (SHRIMATI SARLA MAHESHWARI): Kindly bear with us. 
SHRI R.S. GAVAI: Madam, forget about the pubic distribution system. 
Whatever schemes related to the welfare of poor people like Antyodaya, etc., the 
pre-requisite is that he must have a BPL card, and the real thing is that the BPL 
cards are not given to the BPL people. On the contrary, they are being made 
available to the APL people. Unless and until we find out a mechanism to identify 
the people living below poverty line, thousands of crores of rupees that we are 
spending on various schemes meant for the poor people will be a waste. Thank 
you, Madam.

DISCUSSION ON THE WORKING OF THE MINISTRY OF CONSUMER 
AFFAIRS, FOOD AND PUBLIC DISTRIBUTION-Contd. 
SHRI M.P. ABDUSSAMAD SAMADANI (Kerala): Thank you Madam Vice-
Chairman for giving me an opportunity. 
Madam, I am not here to make a speech. I am making only a few 
suggestions. Various dimensions of the issue on discussion have already 
been covered by hon. Members. Madam, the most important  issue that is 
to be addressed, nowadays by the Ministry, I believe is with regard to the 
Public Distribution Scheme. Now, the Ministry is under the leadership of a 
veteran leader, a very competent Minister, Sharad Pawarji. So, Madam, 
we, as a nation, have great expectations from the hon. Minister in that 
there must be certain very strict measures, instead of promises and 
ideas, and we hope that the hon. Minister would be coming forward with 
certain very strict and immediate steps to curb the situation that poses a 
challenge to the well-being of the nation, with regard to its food and civil 
supplies.  
Madam, I shall now come to the Public Distribution System, which has already 
been mentioned here. Public Distribution System was a very well established 
system. It is one of the great merits of our democracy. That was the condition 
that existed in the country previously. Bu t, the last Government as we all know, 
spoiled the system; they completely ruined 
248 

[3 May, 2005] RAJYA SABHA 
the system and inflicted grave injuries upon the system. For example, the PDS 
that we have in Kerala, we remember it was a gift, reward granted by the late Prime 
Minister, Pandit Jawaharlal Nehru to the State of Kerala. That was running well. 
The ration shop in Kerala was not only a ration shop where the poor people can 
approach; they can purchase commodities of food at a very reasonable rate. But 
more than that, it was a part of the social and cultural life of the people, the 
middle-class people as well as people living below the poverty line. The ration 
shop provided rice, wheat, kerosene and many other essential commodities. 
Very essential commodities were being distributed through the public distribution 
system. But that scene is not at all there now-a-days. We cannot be witness to 
that scene as that was completely demolished by the previous Government. So, I 
would like to know from the hon. Minister what are the steps that are going to be 
taken by the hon. Minister to bring back the PDS to its lost glory. The glory is to 
be reinstated and re-established, especially in States like Kerala. We urge upon 
the Government to take immediate steps to reinstate the conditions that were 
prevailing earlier. 
Then, Madam, black marketing has been discussed with all importance at 
various levels. But we can't understand. what is hurdle. With all our systems 
we are not able to curb the situation; we are not able to control the situation. The 
black market is growing and so also is their bad influence, the tragedies occuring by 
this state of affairs are also growing. The tendency is growing. The process is on an 
upward trend. But the Government, with all its machinery and mechanisms, is not 
able to control the situation. We would like to know from the hon. Minister what are 
the concrete steps with which this growing level of black marketing will be 
controlled. 
Madam, finally, I would like to draw the attention of the hon. Minister to a 
very serious problem. That is the use of poisonous items in food and essential 
commodities, foodgrains. This is an i ssue that has to be addressed with all 
seriousness. Adulteration of food by the so-called business lobbies. Madam, it 
is a very serious problem. Fortunately, ou r hon. Minister is also the Minister for 
Agriculture. So, I think I can humbly draw his attention to the pesticides that are 
used in vegetables and other agricultural products. It has created a condition 
that there is no life in this country. It is  a very serious situation. Everything is 
poisonous. It is more or less as a poet said, जहर की नदी है तू, िफर भी कीमती है 
तू that means, "you are a river of poison, but still you are very precious". Food is 
very precious; it is very essential, but everywhere madam, it is 
249 

RAJYA SABHA [3 May, 2005] 
completely mixed with poision. We would like to know from the hon. Minister in 
our country, not only vegetables but even products like tea, everything is mixed 
with pesticides. Earlier, when we were children, our parents used to tell us to go 
to the market and buy vegetables and fruits from the place where there are no 
flies; if there are no flies, it means it is pure. But now, the situation is such that we 
go to the market and have to buy vegetables and fruits that are infested with flies. If 
flies are not there, it means they are mixed with pesticides. Even flies and 
insects cannot approach food items because of the increasing use of 
pesticides. They are poisonous. There are tea plants in certain areas in South 
India. Tea plants are there where pesticides are used. But there are certain tea 
plants and estates where pesticides are not used, but this tea is directly exported to 
certain Western countries like America.  These imported items from India are 
put to test, and if it is proved that pesticides are not used, only then these 
commodities can enter their country. We are exporting these kinds of things to 
other countries, to foreign countries, and to our people we are giving poisonous 
items. So, I request the hon. Minister and draw his kind attention to this very 
serious state of affairs, with regard to foodgrains, with r egard to vegetable, with 
regard to fruits and with regard to other food items which are very much essential for 
the people. There must be very strict measures from the Government to control 
the situation. Thank you. 
SHRIMATI PREMA CARIAPPA(Karnataka) : Thank you, Madam, for giving 
me this opportunity to speak on this very important subject. Madam, I would like to 
quote Mahatma Gandhi who said, "A customer is the most important visitor on 
our premises. He is not an outsider to our business. He is a part of it. We are not 
doing him a favour by serving him. He is doing us a favour by giving us an opportunity 
to do so." Even Swami Vivekananda had remarked, "Consumer is the king." But 
what is the real picture existing in our country today? Despite reforms, price 
competition is still driven from the. produc er's end and very often the quality is 
something that is compromised upon in order to prosper in business. I feel sorry 
to say that the Indian customer is often taken for granted and is not 
empowered entirely with the producer on the products and services that are 
consumed. This needs to be changed. One of the major commitments of the 
UPA Government under the National Common Minimum Programme is to 
strengthen public distribution system, particularly to the poorest and backward 
sections of the country and also to involve women and ex-servicemen's 
cooperatives in its management. It has also decided to launch 
250 

[3 May, 2005] RAJYA SABHA 
special schemes to make available foodgrains to the most destitutes and infirm. 
Improvements in the functioning of FCI are also high on the agenda of the 
Government. 
The problem facing the country today is  not of shortage of food, but of 
managing the surplus. Ironically, even as the godowns of the FCI are 
overflowing, stray cases of starvation deaths are still being reported. 
Madam, with a network of more than 4.62 lakh fair price shops distributing 
commodities worth more than Rs. 30,000 crore annually to about 160 million 
families, the PDS in India is perhaps the largest distribution network, of its kind in the 
world. This huge network can play a more meaningful role if it ensures the 
availability of food to the poor households. 
But, Madam, all is not well with the PDS. The annual food subsidy involved 
in maintaining the system in huge. The food subsidy Bill for 2002-03 was 
budgeted at Rs. 21,200 crore. It was more than Rs. 25,000 crore in 2003-04. 
And, now this subsidy is Rs. 25,800 crore in 2004-05. But much is needed to be 
done. Shri Rajiv Gandhi remarked in the mid-80's that 'only fifteen paise out of 
rupee one allotted for welfare schemes reached home'. This remark was written off 
as an off-the-cuff remark. But, twenty years later, the Indian bureaucracy is 
endorsing the statement backing it with research and figures. The Planning 
Commission Programme Valuation Division discovered that in 2003-04, more than 
50 per cent, of foodgrains meant to go to the persons below poverty line did not 
reach them. It was pilfered all the way. This means that more than Rs. 4,000 
crores of subsidy for the Targeted Pub lic Distribution Scheme went down the 
drain. In some of the States, the percentage of pilferage is more than 50 per cent. 
In Delhi, the percentage has been found to be around 67 per cent. I am happy 
that the Government is eq ually concerned about addressing the vital issue of 50 
per cent, foodgrains meant for BPL families not reaching them. In fact, the hon. 
Finance Minister has announced in the Budget the Government's intention to 
assess the outcome of expenditure, as huge sums are allotted for the purpose. 
One of the major problems in the existing PDS is the faulty identification of the poor 
resulting in the misplaced targeting of the supply of the subsidised foodgrains. I 
would request the hon. Minister to deal with these issues squarely and 
separately. 
Many Parliamentary reports indicate that there is massive diversion of 
subsidised foodgrains by unscrupulous traders who are in collusion with officials. 
Under the scheme introduced by the previous Government, 30 
251 

RAJYA SABHA [3 May, 2005] 
million tonnes of rice and wheat was exported, at least, on paper. This is the 
worst possible kind of fraud when grains never reached the poor and the starving 
people, instead ended up being sold for high profits. This is quoted from 
National Herald dated 10th October, 2004, under the title 'Massive PDS grain 
diversions'. 
Madam, adding five million more rupees in the Budget to Antyodya Anna 
Yojana is a welcome step from the hon. Finance Minister. The success of this 
scheme depends upon the correct identification of the most vulnerable families 
which are rated as living at the risk of hunger. This will definitely help the needy 
persons to come out of the clutches of hunger. 
The Indian Consumer Protection Act is comparable with the best in the world. 
But, many do not know that there is also system of redress through District, State 
and National Consumer Commissions. We have to promote a larger participation of 
NGOs in the area of awareness of consumer rights. 
Madam, I would like to say a few lines about this teleshopping. Now-a-days, 
distance selling of various services and products has become very popular. 
There are so many sites like baazi.com, indiatimes.com, e-bay. com, which 
are putting various items and services for sale to consumers. Similarly, there are 
regular advertisements of teleshopping on cable TV network. As of now, there is no 
law in India to regulate the distance selling. You may all agree with me that it is very 
difficult to judge the exact nature of the product, say, its colour, texture, design 
by seeing it on a computer monitor or TV screen. Many a time, the product does 
not turn out to be as per your expectations, but since you have ordered it, you 
have to pay even if you do not like it. Although distance selling is prevalent in many 
countries, but, at the same time, consumers have also been given certain 
rights like they can return the product within a specified period without any 
payment if they do not like it. Such rights should be given to the consumer in our 
country also—to return the product within a specified time if he does not like the 
product he ordered for. There should be an obligation on the persons engaged in 
e-selling that they should give the true and exact picture about the product and if 
any consumer finds that there is some wrong information, he should be allowed 
to return the product. Therefore, in order to protect the rights of our consumers, 
we should also go in the direction of having a law on distance selling or make 
appropriate amendments in the Consumer Protection Act. 
I would like to give three, four suggestions regarding the PDS. Madam, I would 
like to suggest the following measures to be adopted immediately to improve the 
management of PDS outlets. 
252 

[3 May, 2005] RAJYA SABHA 
1. The Government may implement the recommendation of the Finance 
Minister regarding independent evaluator in as many as areas and as 
early as possible. 
2. The Government should extend more PDS outlets in rural areas rather 
than in urban areas, as is the case now. 
3. Strict monitoring over the functi oning of the PDS outlets followed by 
some incentives to encourage honesty. 
4. Correct identification of the most vulnerable families to be brought under 
Antyodaya Anna Yojana so that it really reaches the poor 
5. More and more advertisements be given to Consumer Protection Act, to 
educate the consumers and create awareness among them. 
With these words, I once again thank you for having given me an 
opportunity to speak on this subject. 
SHRIN. K. PREMACHANDRAN (Kerala): Madam, Vice-Chairman, first of all, I 
take this opportunity to express my  sincere thanks for having given mean 
opportunity to put across my views in res pect of the working of the Ministry of 
Consumer Affairs, Food and Public Distribution. Madam, this is an important 
Ministry which is having high concerns over the poor people of this country. 
It is an admitted fact that out of more than 100 crores of our population, 36 per 
cent or 26 per cent, whatever it may be, are below the poverty line. Anyway, in 
between 26 and 36, even if we take 30 per cent, it is admitted that 30 per cent of 
the population still lives below the poverty line. 
It is also an admitted fact that 6.52 crore families have been identified as BPL 
families That is the position of the developing country like India So, I fully 
support the views expressed by comrade Mr. Vijayaraghavan. Madam, today we 
have the UPA Government, under the leadership of Dr. Manmohan Singhji. This 
is my humble request that the verdict for the 14th Lok Sabha was not only 
against the communal agenda which was being pursued by the then NDA 
Government, but it was also against the economic reforms which were anti-poor 
and which were being pursued by the then Government. That is why the verdict has 
come. So, my submission is that it is the bounden duty of the UPA Government to 
see that the poor people are benefited, and the Public Distribution System and 
the AAY scheme, as a whole, are strengthened so that the interests of the poor 
people are protected. That is the agenda that is envisaged in the National 
253 

RAJYA SABHA [3 May, 2005] 
Common Minimum Programme also. So, that should be taken care of and we hope 
that the Government will take care of these things. Out of the welfare measures, 
the prime responsibility of the Government is to ensure the food security of the 
country. Madam, food security of the country means security to the common 
people and people living below the poverty line. We are proud to say, and, we have 
to salute the farming community of our country, that we are able to have the food 
sufficiency in our country, we are having record production of surplus food and 
we are having the accumulated stocks also. Record production, the accumulated 
stock, the buffer stocks, everything is there in the godowns of the FCI. But, at 
the same time, we are ashamed to say that in a country, which is having 
surplus food, accumulated stocks, bu ffer stocks, people are also dying of 
starvation and by way of malnutrition. That is also a fact. How can these two 
things co-exist? That is the point that  has to be considered by the Ministry. 
Last time also when these things were discussed during the regime of the 
previous Government, I remember that the then Prime Minister had assured this 
House that the Chief Ministers' conference would be convened so as to discuss 
this very important issue which concerns the poorest of the poor in this country. 
But nothing has materialised so far. So, I would like to ask as to how the deaths 
due to starvation and by way of malnutrition are taking place when we have 
surplus food production, buffer stocks and accumulated stocks, etc: These two 
are coexisting. This is totally contradictory. It proves that the food policy which is 
being pursued by this country, as well as the system which is being followed, is 
faulty. We have to accept that the mechanism which we are following is totally 
faulty. That has to be rectified. Otherwise, these poor people will be put to more 
difficulty. That is my first point. Madam, availability of food is there, but the 
problem is that access to food is not there.  Especially, at the grass-root level, it 
is not there. So, my suggestion is the availability of food and the access to food at 
grass-root level should be the main slogan, which has to be implemented, in the 
food policy of the UPA Government. That is my point. For this, the main thing 
which has to be done is to strengthen the public distribution system. Madam, 
regarding the public distribution system, it is a long-running process of 
procurement, storage, movement and, fi nally, the distribution. Regarding the 
procurement stage, from 1997-98, the Government of India has been 
encouraging the local procurement. That means, decentralisation of the 
procurement is being encouraged. This is a good step; this is a welcome step. 
[MR. DEPUTY CHAIRMAN in the Chair] 
254 

[3 May, 2005] RAJYA SABHA 
Either the State Government or the State Government agencies should have the 
capacity to procure the foodgrains on time. One of the major problems which we 
are facing, as far as the procurement of foodgrains is concerned, is that there is 
no timely procurement of foodgrains. How can it be resolved? The problem can 
be resolved by means of decentralising the procurement process. For this, the 
State has to be strengthened. The infrastructure assistance has to be given by 
the Union Government to have the godowns, to have the procurement facilities, to 
have better roads and all these things. My point is, assistance and guidance 
have to be given by the Union Govern ment so that the States can get 
strengthened, so as to have a timely procurement. In my State, there is an 
experience regarding the procurement of paddy. I appreciate the Government, 
especially, I take this opportunity to congratulate the Minister, finally, the Food 
Corporation of India has come to the picture and procured the paddy. It is a good 
help to the people of Kerala, especially the paddy cultivators. So, my point is, the 
States should be strengthened so that they can have timely procurement and 
this problem can be solved in a little way. My second point is regarding the 
movement and storage. A huge amount of cost is being spent on the 
transportation and storage of the foodgrains. There is a huge pilferage loss. 
Transportation cost is also there. These two factors have to be taken care of in 
handling the public distribution system. Sir, the final stage is the distribution 
stage and this is a very important part in maintaining the f ood security. It is 
admitted that the 6.52 crores BPL famili es are there. My point is, providing 
foodgrains to the poorest of the poor at highly subsidised rates is an important 
milestone in the public distribution system. For this, we have launched the 
programme of AAY. It is very difficult to pronounce, as far as we are concerned. This 
is Antyodaya Anna Yojana. It was launched in December, 2000. The coverage is 
being increased. I would like to congratulate the U PA Government, after assuming 
power, they have increased the coverage from 1.5 crore BPL families to 2 crores 
of BPL families. The amount is also enhanced. That is also an appreciable step. 
This AAY scheme is also found to be a success because it is ensuring the 
availability of the foodgrains at an affordable price to enhance the food security 
in this country. The price, as well as, the quantity also has to be taken. As, Mr. 
Vijayaraghavan has right now said, subsidy has to be increased, in any way. 
Similarly, the Targeted Public Distribut ion System, another poverty eradication 
scheme, which is also being implemented, I think, from 1997 onwards, also 
have some defects. The TPDS as well as AAY, these two schemes are there. 
Many hon. Members have already spoken about the BPL list. That is also a 
255 

RAJYA SABHA [3 May, 2005] 
faulty system, because a person who is otherwise a destitute, he is having an 
electric fan in his thatched house, he will be removed from the list of BPL. So, a 
scientific norm has to be evolved to have a criteria for putting a family in the BPL 
family list. Sir, the norms which are being followed are not scientific norms. 
These norms should be changed. So far as identification of the BPL families is 
concerned, we know that the Panchayati Raj institutions have been entrusted with 
this work in many States. But this is also not a foolproof system. If we have to 
make these two schemes, that is, the AAY and TPDS, successful, we need to 
identify the BPLfamilies honestly, for which I have to make three suggestions. My 
first suggestion is, so far as the BPL and the AAY schemes are concerned, we 
should change the criteria. The criter ia needs to be changed. My second 
suggestion is, the Union Government  should constitute an independent 
regulatory agency to scan the BPLand the AAY schemes. In other words, it 
should be scrutinised and scanned in a strict manner and stringent measures 
should be taken to see that nobody other than the deserving person who is 
eligible for it gets the benefit. If it is done, definitely something will happen. I propose 
for a regulatory mechanism so as to scan, supervise and scrutinise these things. 
My third suggestion is, as I have already said, stringent measures need to be 
taken to see that the beneficiaries are deserving people. As Shri 
Vijayaraghavan said, even after all these welfare and poverty eradication 
schemes, the poorest of the poor are not able to have the foodgrains. That is the 
latest position which is prevailing in the country. What is the reason for this? We 
need to look into it. 
So far as the off-take is concerned—I am not going into the statistics due to 
paucity of time—I have got very interesting figures Sir, 342.73 lakh tonnes was the 
off-take during April—November, 2003 and it had come down to 256.73 lakhs 
during April—November, 2004. There is a very steep decline in the off-take from the 
Central Pool. I am not going into the details of each and every scheme. It means the 
purchasing capacity of the people is not as much as we expect. My point is, the 
purchasing capacity needs to be increased. How it should be increased, I would 
like to make some suggestions. Sir, in the NDA Government's rule of six years, 
there was a record rural unemployment. It has created a very serious situation in 
the country especially in the rural sector. My first suggestion is, you should 
increase the purchasing capacity of the people and enhance the employment 
opportunities. I mean there should be remunerative employment on a regular 
basis. The Food-for-Work-Programme is not sufficient to increase the 
purchasing capacity. Secondly, there should be 
256 

[3 May, 2005] RAJYA SABHA 
an institutional arrangement to distribute foodgrains directly to the starving people. Thirdly, 
our emphasis is always on wheat and rice. The Food Corporation of India and the PDS 
are always giving emphasis on wheat and rice. We are not giving any preference or 
importance to coarse grains which are more cheaper. So emphasis should be shifted from 
wheat and rice to coarse grains. If you can take care of these things, availability and access 
of foodgrains would be better. I would once again say that the poorest of the poor and the 
starving people need to be taken care of. We need to stop the deaths which are taking 
place due to starvation and malnutrition. I once again appeal to the UPA Government 
which is being supported by the Left parties to strengthen the Public Distribution System. The 
Common Minimum Programme very specifically pledges that all subsidies shall be 
targeted towards the poor and truly needy people. I hope this Government will see to it 
that the deserving and truly needy people are protected and their interests are protected 
by strengthening the Public Distribution System. Thank you.

Sir, as many of my previous speakers have said, finally, the Planning 
Commission has accepted the fact that about 50 per cent of the ration which is 
kept for the Public Distribution System  goes into the hands of either the 
exporters or the unscrupulous merchants. It is high time that the Government 
should do something in this regard. On going through the Annual Report of the

ration meant for the Public Distribution System has gone. It has been reported 
even in some of the States that foodgrains meant for the poor has been exported. I 
would like to know from the hon. Minister what action he has taken, as far as 
these things are concerned. Added to this, according to the Report, the top-
heavy management of the Food Corporation of India which is assigned with the 
job of procurement, storage and distribution of foodgrains, about 40 per cent of 
foodgrains handled by the FCI get pilfered and unaccounted for and another 28 per 
cent is eaten away by rodents. Sir, we have been hearing all these things for the 
past decade, but I don't think any action has been taken against these people.

be there as far as BPL is concerned. They should go by regions where poverty and 
backwardness is identified in different places. Sir, many of the speakers have 
spoken very much on the Public Distribution System and food. I would like to 
confine myself to consumer affairs, especially the health-care. 
Globalisation and liberalisation of the economy has brought about a boom in 
consumerism with the consumer exposed to strong and organised market forces 
and corporates. Sir, the Planning Commission, at the 50th National Development 
Council meeting, identified and included Consumer Protection Act, 1986 as one of 
the priority agenda for evolving a national action plan. The Ministry of Consumer 
Affairs, Food & Public Distribution has already submitted an action plan as 
above, which is awaiting the approval of the Planning Commission. 
The consumer has come a long way to protect his rights from the 
malpractices of the corporat e sector, utility sector like Railways and Electricity 
Boards, etc. The consumer courts have been established and district consumer 
rights for are also in operation. More or less, the retail trade of essential 
commodities, cosmetics, medicine, etc., has disciplined itself in line with guidelines 
on display of maximum retail price on packages, the weight, volume of products, 
etc., and also the composition of health beverages, medical preparations, etc. 
Sir, earlier, the medical fraternity, doctors and hospital establishments, were 
kept away from the purview of the Consumer Protection Act because of the nobility 
of a cause with which their profession was identified. They were immune from 
liabilities that other service or production sector were

subjected to, in terms of right value and service for consumer money. 
Moreover, the total spend of an average consumer medicare was less 
compared to other essential commodities and household requisites. 
Sir, now the scenario has undergone a total change. An average consumer 
now spends a large share of his expendable income on medicare. The National Drug 
Pricing Control Authority has enforced strict pricing code for drugs and 
medicines which are printed on the pa ckages. But the multi-national pharma 
companies are charging much in excess of production, overheads, and 
commission on many drugs and medicines. The National Pharma Pricing 
Control Authority is still to come in terms with the costing of such drugs. 
The profession of medicine has been totally commercialised with the element 
of nobility attached to it earlier has evaporated. The medical practiti oner or a 
physician who is enrolled into the profession on an oath of service, to serve the 
humanity is now suspect in the eyes of the common man as an extortionist. Sir, the 
profession has lost its credibility and esteem with which the public held them in the 
yore. 
Despite the Supreme Court's ruling in Indian Medical Association Vs. V.P. 
Shantha, wherein it made reference to  Arizona Vs. Maricope County Medical 
Society wherein two Arizone County medical societies formed two Medical 
Fundations, to promote free-for-service medicine and to provide the community with a 
competitive alternative to existing health insurance plans and by agreement 
amongst the doctors established the schedule of maximum fees that participating 
doctors agreed to accept as payments in full for service performed for patients 
insured under plans, it was held that the maximum fee agreement as price fixing 
agreements are perse unlawful under the Sherman Act, it was observed. Nor does 
the fact that doctors, rather than non-professionals, are the parties to the price fixing 
agreements support the respondents position, the respondents claim for relief from 
the per se rule is simply that the doctors agreement not to charge certain 
insured, more than a fixed price facitities, the successful marketing of an 
attractive insurance plan but claim that the price restraint will make it easier for 
the customers to pay does not distinguish the medical profession from any other 
provider of goods or service. 
Sir, our Supreme Court held that "We are, therefore, unable to subscribe to the 
view that merely because medical practitioner belongs to the medical profession, they 
are outside the purview of the Act and the services rendered by medical practitioners 
are not covered by section 2(1 )(0) of the Act."

Despite this, it is noticed that a larg e number of patients, who are desirous 
of availing medical servies for their ailments are advised to undergo various tests. The 
fact that several of these tests that the patient is compelled to undergo have no 
rational link to the ailment on hand and such tests are conducted as means to earn 
commission from the diagnostic laboratories. What is worse is that some 
expensive tests are being advised to be undertaken by unsuspecting 
consumers. As majority of our country's population being poor and uneducated, 
such unscrupulous means of lining pockets is deplorable. 
The means of sorting out this is by taking stringent action against those 
practitioners who indulge in such sharp practices. My suggestion to the Health 
Ministry and the Consumer Affairs Ministry would be to make it mandatory for all 
medical practitioners who advise diagnostic test to attest a report that such tests 
are necessary along with the reasons for the same under the given fact 
situation. 
Alarmed at the increasing incidence of physicians and hospitals, fleecing the poor 
patients by ordering tests and examinations at prohibitive costs, which in no way 
are essential to the process of diagnosis of simple and common ailments, I 
would suggest the following measures to be enforced. 
There should be a panel of experts, which will continuously determine the 
necessity of such tests and examinations. They should minimise the number of 
such extra investigations. General physicians and medical practitioners who are 
familiar with all aspects of medicine and healthcare should be attending OPDs, 
instead of specialists. Poor patients,  who opt out of going for special 
investigations, should be attended to promptly and given prescription and advice 
based on simple diagnostic procedures. Thank you.

RAJYA SABHA [3 May, 2005] 
Status of Implementation of the recommendations contained in 
the 65th Report of the Department-related Parliamentary 
Standing Committee on Commerce 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF COMMERCE AND 
INDUSTRY (SHRI E.V.K.S. ELANGOVAN): Sir, in pursuance of Directions 73 A of 
the hon. Chairman, Rajya Sabha, issued vide Rajya Sabha Bulletin-Part II dated 
28th September, 2004,1 am making this  statement on the status of the 
implementation of recommendations contained in the 65th Report of the 
Standing Committee on Demands for Grants (2004-05) in respect of 
Department of Commerce. 
(i) Standing Committee examined the Demands for Grants for the year 2004-05 
of the Department of Commerce in its meeting held on 12th August, 2004. The report 
was presented to the Rajya Sabha on 18th August, 2004. The Report contained 31 
recommendations. These recommendations of the Committee mainly relate to 
the timely approval of schemes of Export Credit Guarantee Corporation (ECGC), 
Rubber Plantation Development Scheme, Export Promotion of Spices and Tea 
Plantation Fund, utilisation of funds, review of schemes/specific programmes, 
clearing of pending cases of refund on account of duty drawback on deemed 
exports, formation of Cashew Board, monitoring of the functioning of Agri-Export 
Zones, setting up of more EOUs in the North-East Region, holding of inter-
Ministerial Consultations and consultations with the State Governments, political 
parties and apex industry associations to evolve strategy in the next Ministerial 
Conference of the WTO in Hong Kong, China in December, 2005, etc. 
Out of 31 recommendations, Government has accepted 30 
recommendations. In one case, that is, recommendation made vide paral 3.3 for 
formation of Cashew Board, the Government has not accepted the 
recommendation of the Committee on the grounds that it will not be cost effective. 
Moreover, in the era of globalisation and liberalisation, the trend is towards greater 
autonomy of operations to facilitate trade growth which should be at best left to 
the industry and the private entrepreneurs. 
Out of 30 recommendations accepted by the Government, action has already 
been completed in respect of 25 recommendations. In respect of a 5 cases, action is 
at an advanced stage of completion. These are as follows:- 
a) Para No. 5.2—Launch of Brand Ambassador Network 
b) Para No. 6.5—Amendment in the Foreign Trade 
(Development and Regulations Act, 1992)
